newsitem.title: NEPAL: Enron in talks to build Nepal power plants.
newsitem.headline: Enron in talks to build Nepal power plants.

text.p: A unit of Enron Corp. is in talks with Nepal to develop two hydroelectric plants and export power to India and China, officials said Friday.
They said Houston-based Enron Renewable Energy Corp. wanted to develop the Karnali river hydroelectric project in western Nepal, and the $1.0 billion Arun III project on the Arun river in the east.

The World Bank backed out of a plan to fund Arun III in 1995 due to doubts that the project could be managed efficiently. The dam project had faced opposition from environmentalists, who said it would threaten wildlife.
"We have an interest in the possibility of developing (these projects) on a private sector basis," Robert C. Kelly, Enron Renewable's chief executive officer, said in an interview.
Kelly, in Nepal to explain the company's plan, which was submitted in September, briefed government ministers about it on Friday.
"It is a very preliminary meeting to discuss the concept of developing projects like Arun III and Karnali," Kelly said.
Plans on Arun III were given up after the World Bank stopped an intended $175 million support for the first phase of the project, scheduled to produce 201 megawatts of power.
Nepali officials said India's Tata group had also shown an interest in Arun III.
The other planned project on Karnali is estimated to have a potential to generate 10,800 megawatts of electricity.

"His Majesty's Government is doing the homework for starting a competitive negotiation process for the Karnali mega project," said Dwarika Nath Dhungel, the highest-ranking civil servant in the Water Resources Ministry.
"We will issue a public notice inviting bidders for competitive negotiations before deciding on any party," Dhungel said earlier this week.

Rivers originating in the snow-covered mountains of the Himalayan kingdom are estimated to have a potential to produce 83,000 megawatts of electricity, which the impoverished nation sees as a possible passport to prosperity.
Nepal, which ushered in multi-party democracy under a constitutional monarch in 1990, has invited foreign investors to tap the potential under an economic liberalisation programme.
